Key Research Thinking Patterns: Geospatial Data Fusion for Safety Analytics: Integrating disparate transportation datasets by resolving coordinate system mismatches to enable statistical correlation between infrastructure features and crash outcomes (e.g., Merging Oklahoma Roadway Inventory with NHTSA FARS data using geospatial translation algorithms to perform blackspot and systemic analysis for fatal collision prevention).

Hardware-Aware Context Optimization: Minimizing architectural overhead in multicore systems by designing specialized hardware units that reduce state transition costs to enable efficient thread management (e.g., Implementing a Shared Context Unit (SCU) to reduce context switching latency from tens of thousands of cycles to two cycles in single-chip multiprocessors).

Asymmetric Performance-Power Trade-off Analysis: Evaluating architectural simplifications by leveraging pre-execution results to mask latency in simpler pipeline designs, targeting specific performance gains without the complexity of aggressive out-of-order execution (e.g., Demonstrating that In-Order Runahead with Result Use (IORARU) achieves up to 1.48X speedup over standard in-order pipelines using SPEC CPU2006 benchmarks, offering a lower-power alternative for asymmetric multi-core systems).

Adaptive Quality-of-Service Control for Constrained Networks: Prioritizing spatial fidelity over temporal resolution in video transmission by dynamically adjusting encoding parameters based on network conditions to maintain utility in low-bandwidth environments (e.g., Applying adaptive frame dropping and replication prior to H.264 encoding to improve PSNR and SSIM metrics on low-bandwidth ITS links, ensuring sufficient visual clarity for traffic monitoring despite reduced effective frame rates).
Summary Description: Ronald Barnes is a principal investigator at the University of Oklahoma specializing in the intersection of computer architecture and intelligent transportation systems. His research addresses two primary domains: high-performance, low-power processor design and data-driven road safety engineering. In computer architecture, he develops hardware mechanisms for efficient multicore management, such as Shared Context Units for low-overhead thread migration and runahead execution strategies for asymmetric processors. In transportation engineering, he integrates geospatial data with fatality records to identify crash blackspots and designs connected vehicle prototypes using DSRC and V2V communication for real-time hazard alerting. Additionally, he optimizes video surveillance for ITS by developing adaptive rate control algorithms that enhance spatial quality on low-bandwidth networks. His work bridges hardware innovation and infrastructure safety, leveraging cycle-accurate simulation, geospatial database integration, and vehicular ad hoc network testing to improve both computational efficiency and public safety outcomes.
